analysis.one_liner: Strips legal immunity from social media companies and fines them for banning users over their politics or religion.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and died in committee when the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take away the legal shield (known as Section 230) that currently protects social media companies from being sued over what their users post. It would also make it illegal for companies like Meta, Twitter, and TikTok to suspend or limit a U.S. citizen's account because of the person's social, political, or religious views — even if that person clearly broke the platform's rules against hate speech, harassment, discrimination, or violent threats — with a $5,000 fine for every day the ban lasts. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the clearest winners would be people who want to sue social media companies over content decisions — including users who claim they were banned for their views — and plaintiffs' lawyers, since removing Section 230 opens the platforms to lawsuits over user content. Users who feel they were silenced for their politics would gain a legal tool, with a $5,000-per-day penalty backing it [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It would let people sue social media companies over user-posted content by removing the Section 230 liability protection for large social media services [S2] [S3].

It would make it unlawful for a social media company to suspend, restrict, or reduce the reach of a U.S. citizen's account based on that person's social, political, or religious status, with a civil penalty of $5,000 for each day the restriction continues [S2] [S3].

The ban would apply even when the user clearly violated the company's rules on hate speech, sexual harassment, discrimination, or violent threats, so a banned user could recover penalties regardless of what they posted [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall mainly on the social media companies themselves, which would lose their liability shield and face per-day fines [S2] [S3]. But ordinary users would pay too: platforms could no longer remove accounts for hate speech, harassment, discrimination, or violent threats when the user claims a political or religious basis, so feeds and comment sections would have to carry content that today gets taken down [S2]. Smaller platforms and any online service swept into the bill's broad definition of 'social media service' would face the same lawsuit exposure [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Platforms, and users facing unmoderated content

drawbacks.text: The bill forbids de-platforming 'even if the citizen clearly violates a policy... relating to hate speech, sexual harassment, discrimination, or violent or threatening speech', so platforms would be forced to keep hosting accounts that spew threats or harassment as long as the user frames it as political or religious expression [S2] [S3].

The bill's own definition of a restricted account includes merely 'decreasing engagement' — meaning even quietly downranking a user could trigger a $5,000-per-day penalty, and the defined list of covered companies (Meta, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, Tik Tok) is oddly specific and would not clearly cover new platforms [S3].

Removing Section 230 for large social media services would expose them to suits over essentially any user post, a change critics across the political spectrum have warned would push platforms to either delete huge amounts of legitimate speech or stop moderating altogether (general knowledge about how Section 230 works) [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gestures at a real grievance — people who believe they were banned for their politics — but as written it is a blunt instrument: it bars platforms from enforcing their own rules against hate speech, harassment, and violent threats whenever a user invokes politics or religion, and it attaches a $5,000-a-day penalty to even subtle actions like downranking. The cost to the general quality of online discourse would plausibly outweigh the benefit to the specific people it protects, and the bill's drafting (a fixed list of five companies, no clear threshold for what counts as a 'social media service') suggests it was not built to become law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, got no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote, and expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Santos introduced the Big-Tech Accountability Act of 2023 on April 17, 2023 [S1] [S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died in committee without ever being reported out or coming to a floor vote [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media companies are better off: they kept the Section 230 liability shield and kept the power to enforce their own content rules, including bans for hate speech and violent threats. Users who wanted a legal weapon against platform bans are no better off than before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Social media companies and their moderators

for.name: Rep. George Santos
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 17, 2023; it was his only listed sponsorship vehicle for this measure and it drew no cosponsors. He was expelled from the House in December 2023 after a House ethics investigation and federal fraud charges, which ended any prospect of the bill advancing.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing or markup on it during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted a second member of either party — zero cosponsors — so there was no visible partisan or bipartisan coalition on either side.

industries.industry: Social media platforms (Meta/Facebook, Twitter/X, Instagram, TikTok)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped these companies of their Section 230 liability shield and fined them $5,000 a day for restricting accounts over politics or religion [S2] [S3]. Their interest in keeping the shield and their own moderation discretion largely runs alongside ordinary users' interest in feeds that are free of threats and harassment — though the same shield has also shielded platforms from accountability for harmful content they host.
Removing Section 230 for large social media services would create a stream of lawsuits over user content and de-platforming decisions, with statutory per-day penalties to recover [S2] [S3].
